prize_parts.citation: for credibly identified evidence on how import competition and technology reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: I keep B032 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson as a single-achievement prize. My ballot and trio are unchanged from round 1. I have only narrowed the citation wording, in response to the chair's question about scope. The chair's summary shows four positions with no majority, so the choice cannot rest on support counts. It has to rest on the common criteria. On those, B032 offers the strongest combination of identification credibility and checkability on the list. The core design is transparent: local labour-market exposure to import competition is measured from trade flows and compared across commuting zones. This kind of design can be re-run by others, and it has been re-run, reanalysed and criticised for a decade or more. From my recollection, which I have not re-verified, that scrutiny includes work on the inference properties of shift-share designs (Adão, Kolesár and Morales; Goldsmith-Pinkham, Sorkin and Swift; Borusyak, Hull and Jaravel), a re-estimation of employment effects with an input-output extension (Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Price), and the authors' own update on persistence. The qualitative findings seem to have survived this. Adjustment is slow, exposed workers and places bear lasting costs, and the effects are concentrated locally. The aggregate magnitude has not been settled. That is why the citation should name identified evidence on local labour-market adjustment and should not claim an aggregate number or the whole task-based theory. Dorn also belongs through the technology side. As I recall, Autor and Dorn's polarisation work on low-skill service jobs is a technology contribution as well as a trade one, so the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio covers both halves of the citation more faithfully than a trio with Katz would. The cost is real. Katz's skill-premium work is foundational but is a separate, earlier strand. Including Katz would require a broader citation and would sharpen the Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo attribution problem.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. The conceptual task framework is shared with people outside the credited set (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo), and Acemoglu was recognised in 2024. Katz is excluded, which is a genuine cost. Colleagues who prefer B010, B014 or B016 can fairly say their credit lines are tidier. B010 and B042 have two-person cores. B014 has clearly separable originating contributions, even though it has eight credited names. On the science, the aggregate size and long-run persistence of the China-shock effects remain debated, and shift-share inference has been a live methodological issue. My knowledge of the latest re-examinations is incomplete and unverified here. As a metascience concern, I also note that a prize for this literature honours robust local evidence and a design approach. It does not honour a settled number. Finally, the labour and technology area has had several recent prizes (Card, Angrist and Imbens, Goldin, Acemoglu), and the Committee may weigh timeliness against that.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B014 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as separable building blocks. He treats the post-2021 inflation episode as a test of empirical performance and not of the contribution, and he thinks the Committee should say whether it honours the theoretical strand or the estimation strand.
responses.response: I accept his logic that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is the most defensible conceptual cut. I also accept that the inflation episode tests parameterisation more than the logic of nominal rigidity. A citation confined to nominal-rigidity theory and policy rules answers most of my wording concern, because it makes no forecasting claim. My remaining difference is about what is directly checkable. Much of B014's empirical content is model-dependent, whereas B032's central findings can be compared with data under alternative specifications. I also still see the eight-name credit pool as a legitimacy cost. B014 remains my first alternative. If the Committee converges on it with a citation limited to theory and rules, I would not oppose it on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B032 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She frames the citation around technology and trade shocks with the China-shock evidence as the identified core. She treats Katz as a real cost to exclude and sees Katz's skill-premium strand as distinct and close to Goldin's recognition.
responses.response: I agree with her trio and her wording, and the chair's question about scope pushes me to be explicit. I would keep Katz out because the citation should rest on the identified local-labour-market evidence. The Goldin point seems to me secondary. Goldin's prize was about gender and labour-market history, and Katz was her co-author on the education-technology theme. So the overlap concerns Katz's other work and is not decisive. It does mean that adding Katz would pull the citation toward the broader skill-premium story, which brings the outside-the-list attribution problem back in. I would add one thing to her framing. Dorn's polarisation work with Autor links him to the technology half as well as the trade half, which strengthens the case for crediting him rather than Katz.

responses.point: Teorell moved from B042 to B032 and proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He weights transparent designs that survive re-examination most heavily, but keeps B042 as his first alternative because of its clean two-person credit. He acknowledges that exposure-design inference, magnitude and the 2024 prize proximity are open concerns.
responses.response: We now share a configuration and also a weakness, which is the state of my own knowledge of the re-examinations. The chair asked what evidence supports calling B032 mature. My recollection, unverified here, is that the shift-share inference critiques refined how the designs are interpreted and tested. They did not remove the finding of persistent local costs. The published re-examinations also differ on aggregate employment magnitude, and that is a reason to keep magnitude out of the citation. I agree with him that the 2022 overlap cuts against B042 in a way it does not cut against B032. I also agree that his point that every colleague ranked B032 in their top eight is a weak signal and should not count as merit. I would keep B042 as a fallback and not elevate it. A Kiyotaki-Moore award would fit the three-name limit, and my objection to it is the empirical anchoring of the collateral channel.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B010 with Melitz and Helpman, mainly because its credit line is slightly easier to defend. She holds it less firmly than in her opening because of B032's broad support. She accepts that Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the cleanest credit line within B032, but she is concerned about the Acemoglu and Restrepo overlap.
responses.response: She is right that B010's credit line is cleaner, and I do not claim B032 is better on attribution. I rank it higher because its evidence is more checkable against data. The Pareto assumption and the sufficient-statistics results make the quantitative welfare claims in B010 more assumption-dependent. The mechanism of selection and reallocation is separable from them, though, so a mechanism-only citation of the kind she and Fredriksson propose would answer much of that. I accept that my ranking of B010 below B032 is a judgement and not a decisive scientific difference. The Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum lineage is a real gap, but it is of the same kind as the task-framework gap in B032. What would move me toward B010 is evidence that the identified local-labour-market core cannot be separated cleanly from the task theory in a citation. If I believed that, B010 would be my choice over B032.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B016 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley. He rests the case on the formal framework and on later sharper designs, and not on cross-country regressions. He calls B032 the most serious competing case and would keep Dorn with Autor and Hanson, and he regards Besley's inclusion as the most debatable part of his proposal.
responses.response: His answer to the identification question lowers my reservation about B016. A prize that rests on the formal framework and on later sharper designs is a different object from one resting on cross-country regressions. I still hold observational constitutional evidence to a stricter standard than quasi-experimental local designs. I also see the overlap with the 2024 prize as more material than he does, but I accept that a citation carrying the identification caveats would be acceptable to me. On the Besley point, I would find a Persson-Tabellini pair easier to defend on his own stated criteria, because he concedes that Besley's state-capacity strand is the weakest link. We agree on keeping Dorn. I also agree with his point that the task framework is owed partly to people outside the list, which is why my citation avoids claiming it.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the identified trade-shock evidence and the task-based framework as one achievement or two. If it wants both in the citation, Katz's claim strengthens and the outside-the-list credit problem (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo) becomes harder to avoid.

My recollection of the shift-share inference and persistence literature is incomplete and not verified here. If it turns out that the qualitative local-adjustment findings are less robust than I believe, my ranking of B032 would fall.
Whether the recent labour and technology prizes (Card, Angrist and Imbens, Goldin, Acemoglu 2024) make B032 less timely than macro or trade candidates.

Whether the Committee prefers B014 with a citation confined to nominal-rigidity theory and policy rules, which would address the main objection I have. The eight-name credit pool would remain a legitimacy cost.
Prior-prize facts, such as the 2022 and 2024 prizes and Gertler's status, come from members' stated recollections and have not been independently verified here.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from my supplied profile with respect to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Kiyotaki or Moore. None of them appears among my documented co-authors or collaborators. My methodological interests in replication, many-analyst studies and the Institute for Replication network bear on how I weigh the scrutiny that shift-share designs have received. That is a lens I applied to all candidates, and none of the credited names is a documented co-author or collaborator of mine. My SSE and Stockholm ties to Committee members (Andersson, Friberg, Strömberg) and to former members involve no credited candidate. This is disclosed and not adjudicated.
